### [Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34397>)

This comparative study tests how merging same-base multimodal specialists before on-policy distillation changes the value of initialization, sampling and training objectives. For one Qwen3-VL model family, a uniform merge followed by short full-vocabulary distillation provides a strong integration baseline without coefficient search or elaborate domain schedules.

### [Verifiable On-Policy Distillation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30325>)

VOPD uses the observed correlation between verified rollout outcomes and a teacher’s likelihood preferences to adapt the strength of on-policy distillation. In two Qwen3 mathematical-distillation settings, this improves reported average accuracy over direct imitation and fixed extrapolation, offering a concrete way to use outcome feedback inside dense teacher supervision.

### [On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24809>)

FlashMorph2 selects which Transformer layers retain full attention by sampling discrete hybrid architectures, propagating their own hidden states and adapting shared weights during the selection stage. Under matched subsequent recovery, it improves average long-context and recall scores over FlashMorph across the tested Qwen configurations, providing a practical way to account for interactions that frozen, continuously mixed layer scoring misses.

Actual p.6 Table 1 and p.8 Figure 3/Table 3 directly inspected. Each selection step samples exactly K full-attention layers with Gumbel-Top-K, evaluates the discrete hybrid end to end and jointly updates selection scores and model weights under teacher-to-student vocabulary KL. A budget-preserving sigmoid relaxation with implicitly differentiated threshold supplies a biased straight-through gradient; both attention branches are evaluated for score gradients. Crucially, adapted selection-stage weights are discarded: all compared selected architectures restart from the same layerwise-aligned checkpoint and receive the same recovery. The default 3:1 linear/full budget gives seven full-attention layers in 28-layer Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B; Lightning, GLA and GatedDeltaNet provide six main configurations. Mean RULER rises 63.26→65.68 (+2.42 points), LongBench 29.86→30.94 (+1.08), and six-task recall 48.94→49.70 (+0.76) versus FlashMorph. Appendix tables extend Lightning results to 8B and 30B-A3B. Stage budgets are 320M alignment, 20M selection, 1B logits distillation and 1B long-context finetuning tokens. Selection takes 0.72–3.57 GPU-hours for 0.6B–8B, but costs 1.9–2.4 times FlashMorph selection time. Sole-v1 receipt November 18 17:45:51 UTC, original CL NEW and dated November 19 RECENT, plus the official Eastern schedule support inferred November 19 01:00 UTC manuscript availability. Bounded matching-title/FlashMorph2 artifact searches found no verified prior full release; generic library references are not claimed as author method code.

**Limitations:** On-policy refers to sampled architecture computation/hidden states and adapting shared weights, not sampling new text trajectories. The straight-through architecture gradient is biased and does not establish optimal subset selection. One-time selection GPU-hours exclude alignment and two billion recovery tokens; they are not total conversion or deployment latency/throughput gains. The paper provides no repeated-seed uncertainty for the reported comparisons and some baseline rankings are imported from the earlier FlashMorph study. Averaged benchmark gains do not imply every task improves, and full-attention teacher retrieval remains substantially higher. The continuous-computation ablation is worse than removing both components, so it is not evidence that each component independently gives monotone gains. Exact inference-cost equivalence under the same layer budget is not independently measured here; no dedicated matching author implementation or model release was verified.

### [Folding Language Models into Themselves](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18113>)

New controlled experiments evaluate Concertina, which compresses a pretrained model by repeatedly applying shared blocks with token-dependent low-rank corrections initialized from adjacent teacher layers. The study separates folding topology, token gating and training-data coverage, showing how a smaller stored model can recover much of a teacher's tested capability through distillation. Parameter savings retain the original computation depth and key-value cache, so they do not establish faster inference.

### [Perturbing Inputs Improves Pretraining Distillation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11598>)

The authors improve pretraining distillation by briefly adding token noise or blended inputs to both teacher and student, then returning to ordinary clean-text distillation. Small-model experiments suggest that querying a teacher beyond ordinary training text can improve student learning, with most additive-noise gains coming from perturbing the teacher’s inputs.

### [CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07959>)

CoRD keeps the per-state distillation loss and uses exact coupled sampling from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher policies. Replacing tokens only where the distributions disagree exposes useful training states the student seldom reaches, improving the tested small models’ mathematical reasoning.

### [When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31563>)

AOPD weights teacher guidance by whether the suggested action helps the current student succeed, rather than treating every teacher-preferred token as beneficial. An estimator built from rewarded student rollouts improves several tested math and coding distillation results without extra teacher rollouts or a learned value model, although it requires outcome rewards and does not win every benchmark.

The objective favors teacher actions with positive advantage under student continuations. A change-of-measure estimator combines a sampled teacher/student probability ratio and a dense teacher expectation with a leave-one-out terminal-reward baseline from the same response group. It does not require explicit teacher-action continuation rollouts. Ratio clipping at c=4 caps the teacher measure in both terms without renormalizing it, estimating a modified clipped objective rather than preserving exact unbiasedness for the original unclipped objective. Main comparisons use LoRA rank 64, batch size 32 and non-thinking Qwen models. Paper reward-improvement results concern exact, sufficiently small KL-proximal policy-space updates under their assumptions, not arbitrary finite-sample neural SGD. ### [Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21337>)

STOPD randomly truncates student rollouts at block boundaries and reweights retained token losses to preserve the expected full-rollout gradient sum. Across tested Qwen students and mathematics, coding and instruction-following tasks, the authors report similar accuracy with 25-48% fewer generated tokens and 1.3-2.2x faster training steps, offering a practical way to reduce distillation cost.

**Published:** 2026-10-15 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:05:55.063Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** On-Policy Distillation, Rollout Truncation, Importance Weighting

**Public availability:** 2026-10-16T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21337>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3-5 and relevant Appendices A/B/D-H were inspected. STOPD samples independent cutoffs, rounds each to a block end, and uses exact inverse inclusion probabilities with K=128 after 25 Vanilla warmup steps. The main comparison distills Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 into Qwen3-1.7B-Base over 250 steps, three training seeds and batch 256 on two H100s: reported full-step times are 941 to 513 seconds for math, 566 to 260 for code, and 104 to 80 for instruction following, including generation, teacher scoring, updates and other overhead. Vanilla versus STOPD endpoint aggregate accuracy is 30.1 versus 29.4 for math, 28.5 versus 28.1 for code, and 59.8 versus 60.1 for instruction following. Additional 30B-A3B-teacher experiments use 4B/8B students on two H200/GB200 GPUs respectively. Public availability is inferred as October 16 00:00 UTC from the verified cs.LG new-submission batch and official schedule; the original October 15 06:22:08 UTC receipt date is retained.

**Limitations:** The expected unnormalized gradient and token-count sums are preserved only under budget-invariant generation, prefix-local loss, independent truncation and exact inclusion probabilities. The actual normalized loss uses the previous batch token-count estimate and can retain a scale mismatch; optimizer bounds compare one step from identical parameters and state, not complete training trajectories. Evidence covers Qwen 1.7B-8B students and 250-step runs, with speed depending on rollout length, hardware and scheduling. The weight-free random-truncation ablation also preserves accuracy closely, while inverse weighting better aligns response lengths, so accuracy alone does not prove the weights necessary. No author implementation or model artifact URL was verified; cited Muon code is not a STOPD release.

**Evidence:** technical-report; full-text. The author report supplies reverse-KL pseudocode, reasoning and personalization experiments, and a linked implementation; its June 2026 note documents replacement models in the maintained recipe.

**Limitations:** Teacher quality and token-probability access are prerequisites; some cost comparisons use extrapolated supervised baselines, and the cookbook's replacement models do not themselves reproduce the original numerical results.
